meaning: The third of the Pāṇḍava princes, a son of Indra and Kuntī; the great archer of the Mahābhārata, to whom Kṛṣṇa speaks the Bhagavad-gītā.

phonemes.desc: The j is the palatal “j” of “jump”; the name is related to arjuna, “white, silver”.
Short u as in “put”; the compound flows without stress in the classical cadence.
The final a is a light schwa; the name means “the white one”, “the silvery”.

kin.label: Epithet
kin.form: Pārtha — son of Pṛthā (Kuntī); Kirīṭin — the diademed

kin.label: Father
kin.form: Indra, by Kuntī’s summoning of the king of gods

pronunciation.note: The third Pāṇḍava, to whom Krishna speaks the Bhagavadgītā on the eve of the war.

domains.title: The Third Pāṇḍava, the Great Archer
domains.subtitle: The Warrior Who Doubted, and the Gītā’s Listener
domains.lead: Arjuna is the Mahābhārata’s central hero: the archer without equal, winner of Draupadī’s svayaṃvara, friend and charioteer-client of Krishna, and the man whose crisis on the battlefield became the occasion of the Bhagavadgītā — the moment world philosophy was spoken from a chariot between two armies.

cards.name: The Gandiva
cards.desc: The bow of Brahmā, won from Agni at Khaṇḍava; its twang alone routs armies.

cards.name: The Svayaṃvara
cards.desc: He alone shot the eye of the rotating fish at Draupadī’s bride-choice, looking only at its reflection.

cards.name: The Gītā’s Chariot
cards.desc: Between the armies he faltered — and Krishna answered with eighteen chapters that became a scripture.

cards.name: The Tīrtha Pilgrimage
cards.desc: His year of exile became the Tīrthayātrā — the epic’s encyclopedia of India’s sacred geography.

mythology.lead: Arjuna’s mythology is the epic’s spine: the feats of the forest-years, the disguises of the incognito year, the divine weapons won from Śiva and Indra, and the chariot-dialogue that turned a battle’s morning into the world’s most read scripture. He is the hero who wins everything and is saved, in the end, by having once doubted.

myths.title: The Pāṇḍavas’ Birth
myths.text: When Pāṇḍu was cursed to die at love’s consummation, Kuntī used the boon of the mantra: Dharma fathered Yudhiṣṭhira, Vāyu Bhīma, and Indra himself Arjuna — born, the epic says, with Indra’s marks. The third son was trained by Droṇa, favoured by the master above all pupils, and marked from birth as the one who would carry the war.

myths.title: The Kirātārjunīya
myths.text: In the forest, Arjuna did austerities for the divine weapons; Śiva came as a kirāta, a hill-tribesman, and they fought over a boar’s carcass until the god revealed himself and gave the Pāśupata — the shaft that ends worlds. Kālidāsa made the combat his greatest mahākāvya, the Kirātārjunīya.

myths.title: The Chariot and the Crisis
myths.text: Seeing his teachers and kinsmen ranked against him, Arjuna lowered his bow: ‘I will not fight.’ Krishna’s answer — eighteen chapters on duty, devotion, the self, and action without attachment — is the Bhagavadgītā, the most read and most translated of Sanskrit texts. The war resumed; but the dialogue outgrew it entirely.

myths.title: The Horse and the End
myths.text: After the war, Yudhiṣṭhira’s horse-sacrifice wandered the subcontinent under Arjuna’s guard — his last great circuit. In the Svargārohaṇika, the Pāṇḍavas walk to heaven’s gate; Arjuna falls first among them, his sin named precisely: the vanity of having believed himself the greatest of archers.

lore.syncretism: Arjuna is the Nara of the Nara-Nārāyaṇa pair — the human half of Vishnu’s eternal companion — making his friendship with Krishna a theology in dialogue-form. In Javanese and Balinese tradition he becomes the refined knight of the wayang cycle; and the Gītā made him, doubting, the everyman of all later Indian philosophy.
lore.culturalLegacy: The Gītā’s chariot is the world’s most reproduced scene of instruction; the phrase ‘Kurukshetra’ entered the political vocabulary of every Indian language as the name of any field where duty and doubt collide. His name crowned South Indian kings (Arjunavarman) and the great tank of Rajput legend; and ‘Arjuna award’ is India’s highest honour for a sportsperson — the archer’s prize.
lore.extendedMeditation: Arjuna: the silvery one, the third of five, the hero whose greatest act was a question. Restored plainly, the name holds the Gītā’s whole setting — the bow lowered, the armies waiting, the friend about to become God. Four syllables, one chariot, eighteen chapters.
lore.archaeology: Arjuna’s monuments are the epic’s geography itself — Indraprastha’s Purāṇa Qila in Delhi claims his city; and the wayang kulit’s refined Arjuna puppets of Java are among the finest objects of Indonesian art. The Gītā’s palm-leaf manuscripts number in the millions.
lore.cult: No temple to Arjuna, but his svayaṃvara-archery is the wedding-ceremony’s standard boast, and the Gītā’s recitation is a complete liturgy. The Arjuna-penance reliefs of Mamallapuram’s great bas-relief panel may show his Kirātārjunīya austerities.
lore.iconography: The archer with the Gandiva and the two inexhaustible quivers, Krishna as charioteer before him; the diadem and the ape-banner. His icon is the drawn bow at rest — the moment before the Gītā, frozen forever.
lore.reception: World literature knows him through the Gītā, where he is the eternal student; comparative epic pairs him with Achilles’ rival-enemies and with the archers of every tradition. In modern India he is the sportsperson’s patron, the doubter honoured above the certain — the hero whose question was worth more than his arrows.
